{{Short description|Concept in algebra}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''K''-theory of a category}}
In [[algebraic K-theory|algebraic ''K''-theory]], the '''''K''-theory of a [[category (mathematics)|category]]''' ''C'' (usually equipped with some kind of additional data) is a sequence of [[abelian group]]s ''K''<sub>i</sub>(''C'') associated to it. If ''C'' is an [[abelian category]], there is no need for extra data, but in general it only makes sense to speak of K-theory after specifying on ''C'' a structure of an [[exact category]], or of a [[Waldhausen category]], or of a [[dg-category]], or possibly some other variants. Thus, there are several constructions of those groups, corresponding to various kinds of structures put on ''C''. Traditionally, the ''K''-theory of ''C'' is ''defined'' to be the result of a suitable construction, but in some contexts there are more conceptual definitions. For instance, the ''K''-theory is a 'universal additive invariant' of dg-categories<ref name="dg">{{cite journal|first1=Goncalo|last1=Tabuada|title=Higher ''K''-theory via universal invariants| journal=Duke Mathematical Journal|volume=145|number=1|year=2008|pages=121–206|arxiv=0706.2420|doi=10.1215/00127094-2008-049|s2cid=8886393}}</ref> and [[small category|small]] [[stable ∞-category|stable ∞-categories]].<ref>*{{Cite journal|last1=Blumberg|first1=Andrew J|last2=Gepner|first2=David|last3=Tabuada|first3=Gonçalo|date=2013-04-18|title=A universal characterization of higher algebraic K-theory|journal=Geometry & Topology|volume=17|issue=2|pages=733–838|arxiv=1001.2282|doi=10.2140/gt.2013.17.733|s2cid=115177650|issn=1364-0380}}</ref>

The motivation for this notion comes from [[algebraic K-theory]] of [[ring (mathematics)|rings]]. For a ring ''R'' [[Daniel Quillen]] in {{harvtxt|Quillen|1973}} introduced two equivalent ways to find the higher K-theory. The [[Algebraic K-theory#The_+-construction| plus construction]] expresses ''K''<sub>i</sub>(''R'') in terms of ''R'' directly, but it's hard to prove properties of the result, including basic ones like functoriality. The other way is to consider the exact category of [[projective module|projective]] [[module (mathematics)|modules]] over ''R'' and to set ''K''<sub>i</sub>(''R'') to be the K-theory of that category, defined using the [[Q-construction]]. This approach proved to be more useful, and could be applied to other exact categories as well. Later [[Friedhelm Waldhausen]] in {{harvtxt|Waldhausen|1985}} extended the notion of K-theory even further, to very different kinds of categories, including the category of [[topological space]]s.

== K-theory of Waldhausen categories==
In algebra, the '''S-construction''' is a construction in [[algebraic K-theory]] that produces a model that can be used to define higher K-groups. It is due to [[Friedhelm Waldhausen]] and concerns a category with cofibrations and weak equivalences; such a category is called a [[Waldhausen category]] and generalizes Quillen's [[exact category]]. A cofibration can be thought of as analogous to a [[monomorphism]], and a category with cofibrations is one in which, roughly speaking, monomorphisms are stable under [[Pushout (category theory)|pushouts]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~mitya/langlands/spectra/ktwcss-new.pdf|title=''K''-theory of a Waldhausen category as a symmetric spectrum|last=Boyarchenko|first=Mitya|date=4 November 2007}}</ref> According to Waldhausen, the "S" was chosen to stand for [[Graeme B. Segal]].<ref name=":0" />

Unlike the [[Q-construction]], which produces a topological space, the S-construction produces a [[simplicial set]].

=== Details ===
The [[arrow category]] <math>Ar(C)</math> of a category ''C'' is a category whose objects are morphisms in ''C'' and whose morphisms are squares in ''C''. Let a finite ordered set <math>[n] = \{ 0 < 1 < 2 < \cdots < n \}</math> be viewed as a category in the usual way.

Let ''C'' be a category with cofibrations and let <math>S_n C</math> be a category whose objects are functors <math>f: Ar[n] \to C</math> such that, for <math>i \le j \le k</math>, <math>f(i = i) = *</math>, <math>f(i \le j) \to f(i \le k)</math> is a cofibration, and <math>f(j \le k)</math> is the pushout of <math>f(i \le j) \to f(i \le k)</math> and <math>f(i \le j) \to f(j = j) = *</math>. The category <math>S_n C</math> defined in this manner is itself a category with cofibrations. One can therefore iterate the construction, forming the sequence<math>S^{(m)}C = S \cdots SC</math>. This sequence is a [[spectrum (topology)|spectrum]] called the '''K-theory spectrum''' of ''C''.

==The additivity theorem==
Most basic properties of algebraic K-theory of categories are consequences of the following important theorem.<ref>{{cite journal| first1 = Ross | last1 = Staffeldt | title = On fundamental theorems of algebraic K-theory | journal = K-theory | volume = 2 | issue=4|year = 1989|pages = 511–532 | doi=10.1007/bf00533280}}</ref> There are versions of it in all available settings. Here's a statement for Waldhausen categories. Notably, it's used to show that the sequence of spaces obtained by the iterated S-construction is an [[Spectrum (topology)| Ω-spectrum]]. 

Let ''C'' be a [[Waldhausen category]]. The category of extensions <math>\mathcal{E}(C)</math> has as objects the sequences <math>A \rightarrowtail B \twoheadrightarrow A'</math> in ''C'', where the first map is a cofibration, and <math>B \twoheadrightarrow A'</math> is a quotient map, i.e. a [[pushout (category theory) | pushout]] of the first one along the zero map ''A'' → ''0''. This category has a natural Waldhausen structure, and the [[forgetful functor]] <math>[ A \rightarrowtail B \twoheadrightarrow A' ] \mapsto (A, A')</math> from <math>\mathcal{E}(C)</math> to ''C'' × ''C'' respects it. The '''additivity theorem''' says that the induced map on K-theory spaces <math>K(\mathcal{E}(C)) \to K(C) \times K(C)</math> is a homotopy equivalence.<ref>{{cite book | last = Weibel | first = Charles | author-link = Charles Weibel | title = The K-book: an introduction to algebraic K-theory | publisher = AMS | series = Graduate Studies in Mathematics | volume = 145 | year = 2013 | chapter = Chapter V: The Fundamental Theorems of higher K-theory}}</ref>

For [[dg-category | dg-categories]] the statement is similar. Let ''C'' be a small pretriangulated dg-category with a [[semiorthogonal decomposition]] <math>C \cong \langle C_1, C_2 \rangle</math>. Then the map of K-theory spectra K(''C'') → K(''C''<sub>1</sub>) ⊕ K(''C''<sub>2</sub>) is a homotopy equivalence.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Tabuada | first = Gonçalo | title = Invariants additifs de dg-catégories | journal = International Mathematics Research Notices | volume = 2005 | issue = 53 | year = 2005 | pages = 3309–3339| arxiv = math/0507227 | doi = 10.1155/IMRN.2005.3309 | bibcode = 2005math......7227T | doi-access = <!-- Not free-->| s2cid = 119162782 }}</ref> In fact, K-theory is a universal functor satisfying this additivity property and [[Morita equivalence | Morita invariance]].<ref name="dg" />

== Category of finite sets==

Consider the category of [[Glossary of category theory#P|pointed]] finite sets.  This category has an object <math display="inline">k_+ = \{0, 1, \ldots, k\}</math> for every [[natural number]] ''k'', and the morphisms in this category are the functions <math display="inline">f : m_+ \to n_+</math> which preserve the zero element.  A theorem of [[Barratt–Priddy theorem|Barratt, Priddy and Quillen]] says that the algebraic K-theory of this category is a [[sphere spectrum]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hEDjmKdyFAAC|title=The Local Structure of Algebraic K-Theory|last1=Dundas|first1=Bjørn Ian|last2=Goodwillie|first2=Thomas G.|last3=McCarthy|first3=Randy|date=2012-09-06|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4471-4393-2|language=en}}</ref>

==Miscellaneous==

More generally in abstract category theory, the K-theory of a category is a type of [[categorification|decategorification]] in which a set is created from an equivalence class of objects in a stable (∞,1)-category, where the elements of the set inherit an [[Abelian group]] structure from the [[exact sequence]]s in the category.<ref name="KT">{{cite web|title=K-theory in nLab|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/K-theory#idea|website=ncatlab.org|access-date=22 August 2017}}</ref>

=== Group completion method ===
The [[Grothendieck group]] construction is a functor from the category of rings to the category of abelian groups. The higher ''K''-theory should then be a functor from the category of rings but to the category of higher objects such as [[simplicial abelian group]]s.

=== Topological Hochschild homology ===
Waldhausen introduced the idea of a trace map from the algebraic ''K''-theory of a ring to its [[Hochschild homology]]; by way of this map, information can be obtained about the ''K''-theory from the Hochschild homology. Bökstedt factorized this trace map, leading to the idea of a functor known as the topological Hochschild homology of the ring's [[Eilenberg–MacLane space|Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Schwänzl|first1=R.|last2=Vogt|first2=R. M.|last3=Waldhausen|first3=F.|date=October 2000|title=Topological Hochschild Homology|url=https://pub.uni-bielefeld.de/download/1785323/2314834|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society|volume=62|issue=2|pages=345–356|issn=1469-7750|doi=10.1112/s0024610700008929|s2cid=122754654 }}</ref>

=== K-theory of a simplicial ring ===
If ''R'' is a constant simplicial ring, then this is the same thing as ''K''-theory of a ring.
